- **Ethnic composition:** Large waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant labor, per Wikipedia
- **Key historical events:** Rapid industrial growth and immigration tied to the steel boom; Pittsburgh annexed the independent city of Allegheny City in 1907 (after this period but relevant to where earlier Allegheny City records are filed)

## Boundary changes
Allegheny County's own boundaries were stable through this period (formed 1788, no record of courthouse disasters per the wiki page's Record Loss note). Note, however, that Pittsburgh and Allegheny City were separate incorporated cities until 1907 - records for Allegheny City residents before that date were created and are indexed under "Allegheny City," not "Pittsburgh."

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County level 1852-54 and 1893 for births and deaths, 1789 for marriages; statewide registration of births and deaths began January 1906 with general compliance by 1915; statewide marriage registration from 1885 (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:** County marriages 1885-1950 (collection 1921317, FamilySearch), civil marriages 1677-1950 (1571957), compiled marriages 1700-1900 (1502909), death certificates only from 1906 onward (2255317)
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Register of Wills holds marriage records; the county's Department of Court Records holds other vital/court series (county wiki page)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth/death civil registration exists for most of the 1870-1900 target window - this is the single biggest limitation for this period; rely on church records and the 1906+ run for late-period deaths
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial records; see Church records below

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Wide range tied to immigrant groups (Catholic parishes for Irish/Polish/Slovak/Croatian/Italian communities, Protestant and Lutheran congregations for German communities) - see the dedicated Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Church Records wiki page (linked from the county page) for denomination-level detail, not retrieved in this survey
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials typically predate or run parallel to civil registration
- **Where held:** Individual parish/congregation archives; FamilySearch microfilm holdings per the county page
- **Gaps:** This survey did not retrieve the denomination-by-denomination Church Records subpage; consult it directly for specific parish coverage

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Standard decennial federal census 1870, 1880, 1890 (largely destroyed/lost nationally), 1900 all apply
- **Local digitized schedules:** University of Pittsburgh's Historic Pittsburgh site has digitized U.S. Census Schedules for Allegheny City (1850, 1860, 1870) and Pittsburgh (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) only - no coverage elsewhere in the county (county wiki page, Census Records section)
- **Mortality schedules:** Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules 1850-1880, index & images, FamilySearch collection 3512181 - useful substitute for pre-1906 death data
- **Access:** Indexed & imaged for the mortality schedules; the Pitt digitized schedules are a browsable local resource outside FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills (Register of Wills), administrations, guardianship (Orphan's Court), civil/criminal (Prothonotary, Court of Common Pleas)
- **Date range:** From 1788 per the county's "Known Beginning Dates" table
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Courthouse, 436 Grant St., Pittsburgh; also FamilySearch collection 1999196, Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 (browse-only per volume_search, imageGroupNumber 008120441, 0% indexed, 1180 images)

### Land records
- **Types:** Deeds held by the Recorder of Deeds; land records date from 1788 per the county page
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Courthouse; not separately surveyed here

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** None of the major U.S. wars fall within 1870-1900 itself, but Civil War pension files (for older generation) and later records are at the National Archives
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3 also carries Pittsburgh-specific material (see Directories)

### Occupational and industrial records (steel industry focus)
- **Company employment records:** Pennsylvania, U.S. Westinghouse Employment Records, 1890-1953, Ancestry collection 63266, index & images (subscription); Pennsylvania U.S., Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania, 1890-1973, Ancestry collection 62557, index & images - includes records for Jones & Laughlin Steel Corporation (both per the county wiki page, Business, Commerce, and Occupations section)

- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery named specifically, with its own genealogy name-search page

- Not independently surveyed this run; the FamilySearch Wiki's newspaper coverage for the county was not fetched. Newspapers.com is a curated external link FamilySearch returns for Pennsylvania generally.

- **Relevant ports:** Pittsburgh is inland, but naturalization and alien-registration records were filed locally regardless of port of entry

**Philadelphia, 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic — Records & Repositories**

Because Pennsylvania had no statewide vital registration until 1906, the 1793 epidemic deaths were never captured as modern "vital records." The key record types and repositories to target are:

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia City and County, established 1682 (place_search dateRange +1682/).
- **County seat / administrative center:** City of Philadelphia.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania.
- **Population during period:** Not returned by place_population in this run (tool gap).
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port and U.S. capital (1790-1800) - shipping and commerce, which made it a yellow fever entry point.
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic, August-November 1793, killed roughly 5,000 people (about one-tenth of the city's population). Mayor Matthew Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush left detailed accounts; records of the dead and relief efforts are held by the Philadelphia City Archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and church archives (Wikipedia, 'Yellow fever epidemic of 1793', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793).

## Boundary changes
Not assessed in this run - place_search_all returned no results for Philadelphia County; the city and county were later consolidated in 1854, outside the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania's statewide civil death-certificate collection on FamilySearch begins 1906 (collections_search: 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968'); no statewide civil registration covered 1793.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil vital records for the epidemic; rely on church burial registers and municipal relief/death records (see Church records and Other record types below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers; the Guardians of the Poor/Committee records described below.

### Church records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials recorded by individual congregations; several Philadelphia congregations kept burial registers through the 1793 epidemic (per Wikipedia summary above), which is the primary record class for deaths in this event since no civil death registration existed yet.
- **Where held:** Individual church/denominational archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (per Wikipedia).
- **Gap:** This survey did not identify specific digitized Philadelphia church burial registers for 1793 - catalog_search returned 0 hits and the FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched returned only generic content, not Philadelphia-specific holdings.
- **Related holding found:** volume_search located a digitized, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) volume of 'Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes' covering 1750-1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images, English) - Quaker meeting minutes, not a burial register per se, but may record deaths/disownments/relief among Quaker families during the epidemic.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 federal census exists (three years before the epidemic); the 1790 Pennsylvania schedule was largely lost/reconstructed, and no mid-decade enumeration covers 1793 directly - use 1790 and 1800 as bracketing snapshots.
- **Access:** Not detailed by collections_search in this run beyond the statewide marriage/probate/death collections listed below; consult Repository guide.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories - an epidemic that killed ~5,000 in a few months produced a surge of sudden/intestate deaths, making probate and administration filings especially valuable for 1793.
- **Date range:** collections_search found 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196), which spans 1793, though its indexed person_count returned 0 in this run.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County probate court / Register of Wills; also described generically by the FamilySearch Wiki fallback page as held at county courthouse or state archives.

### Land records
- Not specifically surveyed for 1793; county deed records would be held at the Philadelphia County Recorder of Deeds per the generic FamilySearch guidance retrieved (no Philadelphia-specific land page was returned in this run).

### Military records
- Not directly relevant to the 1793 epidemic; omitted as the epidemic itself is a civilian public-health event, not a conflict.

### Cemetery records
- Burial grounds used during the epidemic (e.g., congregational burial yards) are referenced generally by the Wikipedia summary; no FindAGrave/BillionGraves-specific Philadelphia count was returned by this run's tools, though findagrave.com appears in the curated external links below.

### Newspaper records
- Philadelphia newspapers of 1793 (e.g., contemporary accounts by Mathew Carey and others) are referenced by historical sources but not confirmed by a tool result in this run; newspapers.com appears in curated external links below as a general resource.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Philadelphia was a major port; passenger arrivals are a NARA record class per the generic FamilySearch guidance. Not epidemic-specific; included for completeness since the city's status as a port is part of why the fever arrived (traced by historians to refugees from Saint-Domingue).

### Other record types
- **Municipal/relief records:** Per the Wikipedia summary, the 'Committee appointed by the citizens' (the 1793 relief committee under Mayor Matthew Clarkson) kept minutes documenting relief efforts and deaths, held along with other civic material at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. These were not independently confirmed by a FamilySearch tool in this run - treat as a lead to pursue directly with those repositories.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (id 1999196); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (id 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (id 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750-1800 (browse-only volume) | No statewide 1793 civil vital records exist, so FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records category (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Category:Vital_Records) is the index point for whatever substitute church/probate material is cataloged | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | No mid-decade 1793 enumeration exists; 1790/1800 census bracket the epidemic | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Fills the gap in confirmed FamilySearch burial-register holdings for individual 1793 epidemic deaths | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Fills the gap in confirmed newspaper-specific coverage of the epidemic in this survey | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Not epidemic-specific; listed because returned as a curated resource for this place | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives and Records Administration (https://www.archives.gov/) | Fills the gap in confirmed passenger-list/port-of-entry holdings | Free |

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia City and County, established 1682 (place_search dateRange +1682/).
- **County seat / administrative center:** City of Philadelphia.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania.
- **Population during period:** Not returned by place_population in this run (tool gap).
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port and U.S. capital (1790-1800) - shipping and commerce, which made it a yellow fever entry point.
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic, August-November 1793, killed roughly 5,000 people (about one-tenth of the city's population). Mayor Matthew Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush left detailed accounts; records of the dead and relief efforts are held by the Philadelphia City Archives, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and church archives (Wikipedia, 'Yellow fever epidemic of 1793', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793).

## Boundary changes
Not assessed in this run - place_search_all returned no results for Philadelphia County; the city and county were later consolidated in 1854, outside the target period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania's statewide civil death-certificate collection on FamilySearch begins 1906 (collections_search: 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968'); no statewide civil registration covered 1793.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil vital records for the epidemic; rely on church burial registers and municipal relief/death records (see Church records and Other record types below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers; the Guardians of the Poor/Committee records described below.

### Church records
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials recorded by individual congregations; several Philadelphia congregations kept burial registers through the 1793 epidemic (per Wikipedia summary above), which is the primary record class for deaths in this event since no civil death registration existed yet.
- **Where held:** Individual church/denominational archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (per Wikipedia).
- **Gap:** This survey did not identify specific digitized Philadelphia church burial registers for 1793 - catalog_search returned 0 hits and the FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched returned only generic content, not Philadelphia-specific holdings.
- **Related holding found:** volume_search located a digitized, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) volume of 'Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes' covering 1750-1800 (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images, English) - Quaker meeting minutes, not a burial register per se, but may record deaths/disownments/relief among Quaker families during the epidemic.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1790 federal census exists (three years before the epidemic); the 1790 Pennsylvania schedule was largely lost/reconstructed, and no mid-decade enumeration covers 1793 directly - use 1790 and 1800 as bracketing snapshots.
- **Access:** Not detailed by collections_search in this run beyond the statewide marriage/probate/death collections listed below; consult Repository guide.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories - an epidemic that killed ~5,000 in a few months produced a surge of sudden/intestate deaths, making probate and administration filings especially valuable for 1793.
- **Date range:** collections_search found 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196), which spans 1793, though its indexed person_count returned 0 in this run.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia County probate court / Register of Wills; also described generically by the FamilySearch Wiki fallback page as held at county courthouse or state archives.

### Land records
- Not specifically surveyed for 1793; county deed records would be held at the Philadelphia County Recorder of Deeds per the generic FamilySearch guidance retrieved (no Philadelphia-specific land page was returned in this run).

### Military records
- Not directly relevant to the 1793 epidemic; omitted as the epidemic itself is a civilian public-health event, not a conflict.

### Cemetery records
- Burial grounds used during the epidemic (e.g., congregational burial yards) are referenced generally by the Wikipedia summary; no FindAGrave/BillionGraves-specific Philadelphia count was returned by this run's tools, though findagrave.com appears in the curated external links below.

### Newspaper records
- Philadelphia newspapers of 1793 (e.g., contemporary accounts by Mathew Carey and others) are referenced by historical sources but not confirmed by a tool result in this run; newspapers.com appears in curated external links below as a general resource.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Philadelphia was a major port; passenger arrivals are a NARA record class per the generic FamilySearch guidance. Not epidemic-specific; included for completeness since the city's status as a port is part of why the fever arrived (traced by historians to refugees from Saint-Domingue).

### Other record types
- **Municipal/relief records:** Per the Wikipedia summary, the 'Committee appointed by the citizens' (the 1793 relief committee under Mayor Matthew Clarkson) kept minutes documenting relief efforts and deaths, held along with other civic material at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. These were not independently confirmed by a FamilySearch tool in this run - treat as a lead to pursue directly with those repositories.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (id 1999196); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (id 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (id 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750-1800 (browse-only volume) | No statewide 1793 civil vital records exist, so FamilySearch Wiki Vital Records category (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Category:Vital_Records) is the index point for whatever substitute church/probate material is cataloged | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | No mid-decade 1793 enumeration exists; 1790/1800 census bracket the epidemic | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Fills the gap in confirmed FamilySearch burial-register holdings for individual 1793 epidemic deaths | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Fills the gap in confirmed newspaper-specific coverage of the epidemic in this survey | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Not epidemic-specific; listed because returned as a curated resource for this place | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives and Records Administration (https://www.archives.gov/) | Fills the gap in confirmed passenger-list/port-of-entry holdings | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 matching digitized volume for Pennsylvania 1750-1800 (the Quaker meeting minutes); catalog_search returned 0 hits; this is not a complete survey of Philadelphia's 1793 holdings, only what these two tools returned in this run.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia City Archives | Records of the dead and relief efforts from the 1793 epidemic, per Wikipedia | In-person / contact archives directly (not detailed by a FamilySearch tool in this run) |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Records of the dead and relief efforts, detailed accounts by Clarkson and Rush, per Wikipedia | In-person / contact repository |
| Church/denominational archives | Burial registers for congregations active in 1793 | In-person / contact archives; specific congregations not confirmed by tool results |

## Records NOT online
No tool result in this run confirmed which, if any, of the Philadelphia City Archives' or Historical Society of Pennsylvania's 1793 epidemic-specific holdings (death registers, Committee minutes) are digitized or online. Treat them as physical-repository-only until confirmed otherwise.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this run stated that any specific 1793 Philadelphia record set was destroyed or lost. The 1790 federal census for Pennsylvania is widely known to survive in only reconstructed/partial form, but this was not independently confirmed by a tool result in this run, so it is noted as context only.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched for Philadelphia and Pennsylvania in this run (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) all returned the same generic fallback content rather than place-specific articles; a wiki_search for 'Philadelphia 1793 yellow fever epidemic' did locate two live section references - 'Philadelphia Genealogy' > 'Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793' and 'Philadelphia Genealogy' > 'Church Records' (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) - but reading that URL also returned only the generic fallback page in this run; retry this page directly.
- Because no civil death registration existed in 1793, prioritize church burial registers and the Committee/Guardians of the Poor relief records over any vital-records search.
- A sudden-death event of this scale often shows up first in probate (administration) filings rather than wills, since many deaths were unexpected - search Philadelphia County administrations for 1793-1795.
- Cross-check Quaker Philadelphia Yearly Meeting minutes (1750-1800, browse-only, 145 images, imageGroupNumber 001188322) for Quaker families, since Quakers were prominent in the city's relief efforts.
- Contact the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania directly, since this survey's tools did not return digitized/indexed versions of the epidemic-specific civic records they are reported to hold.

# Locality Guide: Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Focus on the October 1871 Great Fire

## Jurisdiction Overview
Chicago sits within Cook County, Illinois. The Cook County Courthouse was the central repository for the city's official records — and it burned in the fire of October 8–10, 1871, which killed roughly 300 people, destroyed ~3.3 square miles, and displaced over 100,000 residents. The fire consumed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls, creating a profound gap in Chicago's pre-1871 genealogical record. The Burnt Records Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register destroyed deeds, and Chicago Title and Trust Company's records became a key substitute for pre-fire property ownership.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Illinois, Cook County, **Birth Certificates, 1871–1940** (FamilySearch collection 2024189)
- Illinois, Cook County, **Death Records, 1871–1947** (FamilySearch collection 1913456)
- Illinois, Cook County, **Marriage Records, 1871–1920** (FamilySearch collection 1756321)

All three collections start in 1871 — consistent with the courthouse destruction. No indexed civil vital records predating the fire were found in this survey.

### Church Records *(Best substitute for pre-1871 vital events)*
- **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925** (FamilySearch collection 1803978)
  Spans well before and after the fire, making it the strongest substitute for lost pre-fire births, marriages, and deaths. Many Chicago congregations of this era were immigrant (especially German), so some registers may be in languages other than English.

### Court and Land Records
Two digitized volumes were located in this survey:
| Volume | Description | Date Range | Images | Indexing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 009982110 | Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies) | 1865–1871 | 38 | 0% — browse only |
| 009982111 | Post-fire Property Re-recordings | 1871–1880 | 112 | 41% indexed |

Work these two volumes together as a continuous land-record trail — the second exists specifically because of losses documented in the first.

### Census Records
- **1870 federal census** — the last full pre-fire snapshot of a Chicago household
- **1880 federal census** — the first full post-fire snapshot

These two censuses bracket the disaster and are especially important for Chicago research.

### Newspapers
Newspapers of 1871 carry fire-related casualty lists, relief rolls, and property-loss notices — a named external source for this purpose is Newspapers.com (subscription). No FamilySearch-indexed newspaper collection for this period was returned in this survey.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What it covers | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church records (1833–1925), civil vital records (1871+), two digitized court/land volumes | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (casualty lists, relief notices, obituaries) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal census, naturalization, military records | Free/in-person |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Cook County Clerk/Recorder of Deeds | Post-fire re-recorded deeds and current courthouse records |
| Chicago Title and Trust Company (or successor) | Pre-fire property ownership abstracts — a key substitute source; not found indexed online in this survey |
| Chicago History Museum | Fire-related artifacts, relief rolls, local history collections |

---

## Known Record Losses
The Great Chicago Fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, taking with it the city's official deeds, birth/death/marriage registers, court records, and tax rolls. No "missing-but-extant" originals of those pre-1871 civil series should be expected to surface online. The substitutes are:
1. **1833–1925 church records** (spans the loss)
2. **Post-fire re-recorded property volume** (the Burnt Records Act process)
3. **Insurance/title company records** (Chicago Title and Trust Co.)

---

## Research Tips
1. **Start with church records** — the 1833–1925 Cook County church collection is the strongest substitute for lost pre-fire vital events.
2. **Use the two censuses as brackets** — the 1870 census shows the family before the fire; the 1880 census shows where they landed afterward.
3. **Work the land-record volumes as a pair** — the pre-fire reconstructed copies and the post-fire re-recordings tell one continuous story of a property.
4. **Contact Chicago Title and Trust Company directly** for pre-fire property abstracts; this material was not found in any online index in this survey.
5. **The FamilySearch catalog returned zero hits** for Cook County, Illinois in this survey — that is a cataloguing gap, not proof no material exists. Directly contacting the Cook County Clerk/Recorder or the Chicago History Museum is warranted.

---

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
French Louisiana (*La Louisiane*) was an administrative district of New France. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville and served as the colonial capital. France controlled the territory 1682–1762, then ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762). Spain administered the colony until secretly retroceding it to France in 1800; Napoleon then sold it to the United States in 1803. Researchers must expect a **language and record-custody shift mid-period** — French administration through ~1769, Spanish thereafter.

The colony operated under the *Code Noir*, which required Catholic baptism of enslaved people. Vital events were recorded by the Catholic Church and the Superior Council.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No statewide civil registration existed during the French colonial period.** The earliest statewide index on FamilySearch begins in 1819, well after this era.
- **Primary substitute:** Catholic parish sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials).

### Church Records *(most important record type for this period)*
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic — the established church under both French and Spanish rule.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials (sacramental registers).
- **FamilySearch collections found:**
  - "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection id 1612905, ~987,654 people)
  - FamilySearch image group **004330991** — *Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, 1720–1803* (264 images, **0% name-indexed**, browse-only)
- **Language:** French (pre-1769) and Spanish (post-1769), reflecting the change in colonial administration.
- **Gap:** No collection covering church records before 1718 was located in this survey.

### Superior Council (Notarial / Court) Records
- The Superior Council (*Conseil Supérieur*) handled all colonial legal, notarial, and estate business — the colonial-era equivalent of court, probate, and land records combined.
- **FamilySearch image group 004330992** — *French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), Louisiana, 1699–1769* (149 images, **0% indexed**, browse-only, in French/Spanish)
- These records are the closest analog to what later became courthouse records.

### Probate Records
- "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (FamilySearch id 2078341, ~456,789 people) overlaps the tail of this period (1756–1803).

### Land Records
- A FamilySearch Wiki page, "Louisiana Land and Property," includes a **Colonial Land Grants** section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) worth reading; specific holdings or repositories were not confirmed in this survey.

### Census Records
- No French or Spanish colonial census/enumeration collection was returned by any tool in this survey. U.S. federal censuses begin in 1790, before Louisiana was part of the U.S.

### Military Records
- No colonial French/Spanish military or militia collection was identified.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What it holds for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records 1718–1925 (indexed); Archdiocese of New Orleans sacramental registers 1720–1803 (browse-only images); Superior Council notarial acts 1699–1769 (browse-only images); Probate records from 1756 | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** (archives.gov) | General federal records resource; not colonial-specific | Free |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records generally | Free |

---

## Records NOT Online / Not Searchable
- Both digitized colonial volumes (church registers and Superior Council acts) are **browse-only images with no name index** — finding an ancestor requires paging through images, not typing a name.
- Pre-1718 parish registers were not located online in this survey.
- Colonial land grants may not be fully digitized — not confirmed.

## Known Record Losses
No specific colonial record series was confirmed destroyed or lost by the tools used in this survey. Treat gaps as unconfirmed coverage, not established losses.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Browse image by image.** Both major colonial series on FamilySearch (image groups 004330991 and 004330992) are unindexed — plan to page through them rather than search by name.
2. **Read both French and Spanish.** Records shift from French to Spanish around 1769 when Spain took effective control. Some knowledge of period handwriting (*Kurrentschrift* is less relevant here than French cursive and Spanish secretary hand) will help.
3. **Search New Orleans first.** Colonial records for the whole territory centered on New Orleans through 1803, so look there regardless of where in Louisiana the family lived.
4. **Follow the land grants lead.** The FamilySearch Wiki's Louisiana Land and Property page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) was located but not read in full — it may point to additional repositories.
5. **Check the FamilySearch Wiki directly** for Louisiana vital records and church records pages, as the specific Wiki pages did not fully load in this survey.

---

**Summary:** Louisiana's French colonial period left behind mainly Catholic Church sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) and Superior Council notarial acts, written first in French and later in Spanish. Both major series survive as digitized but unindexed images on FamilySearch — finding a specific family means browsing pages rather than searching by name. No government civil registration existed. The best starting points are FamilySearch image groups **004330991** (Archdiocese of New Orleans church records, 1720–1803) and **004330992** (Superior Council notarial acts, 1699–1769), along with the indexed "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" collection.

- **Religious context:** The colony operated under the Code Noir (Black Code), which regulated slavery and required Catholic baptism of enslaved people. Colonial vital events were recorded by Catholic parishes and by the Superior Council.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania anthracite coal region (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- Formed 1811. County seat: Pottsville. Part of Pennsylvania's anthracite coal belt alongside Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (Wikipedia: Coal mining in Pennsylvania).
- Economy: anthracite coal mining, dominated by companies such as the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and the Lehigh Valley Coal Company.
- Ethnic composition: large immigrant mining workforce - Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian.
- Key historical events: Molly Maguires activity in the 1870s; the 1869 Avondale Mine disaster (Luzerne County) prompted the state's first mine safety legislation.
- Population figures for Schuylkill County 1870-1900 could not be confirmed - place_population returned no data in this survey.

## Boundary changes
Schuylkill County has existed with stable boundaries since its 1811 formation (place_search dateRange '+1811/'); no boundary change was identified for 1870-1900.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Vital Records page could not be retrieved with jurisdiction-specific content in this survey (it returned a generic fallback page); the start date and level of Pennsylvania birth/marriage/death civil registration could not be confirmed here. Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (collection 2255317) is indexed on FamilySearch but begins after this period. Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 1571957) and Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (collection 1921317) overlap the period.

### Church records
A collection titled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) was returned by collections_search; its person_count and labeling as a test fixture make it worth confirming directly before relying on it. Given the area's immigrant mix, Catholic (Irish, Polish, Slovak, Italian), Welsh/German Protestant, and Lithuanian congregations are likely present, but this survey did not confirm specific parish names or founding dates - check denominational archives and FamilySearch microfilm holdings.

### Census records
Federal census (1870, 1880, 1900 - 1890 largely destroyed nationally) is the main enumeration; this survey did not confirm a Pennsylvania state census for this period.

### Probate and court records
Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) covers the period but shows a person_count of 0 in this survey's results - treat as present but not yet indexed with named persons; likely held at the county courthouse (Schuylkill County).

### Land records
No collections_search or catalog_search hits returned land/deed collections specific to Schuylkill County in this survey; county courthouse deed books are the standard repository for Pennsylvania land records.

### Military records
No period-specific military collections were returned; Civil War-era pension and service records for this period would be at NARA.

### Cemetery records
No FamilySearch collection or catalog hit named a specific Schuylkill cemetery; Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/, from external_links_search) is a starting point for coverage.

### Newspaper records
Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, from external_links_search) was returned as a curated resource; no Schuylkill-specific title or date range was confirmed in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
Given the heavy immigrant mining population, passenger lists and naturalization records (pre-1906, filed in any court of record) are relevant; NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was the curated resource returned.

### Mining-specific records (industry-specific, found this survey)
volume_search located: (1) imageGroupNumber 002240015, Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County, 1870-1900, 410 images, 95% name-indexed and full-text searchable; (2) imageGroupNumber 002240016, Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870-1895, 287 images, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable); (3) imageGroupNumber 002240017, Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878-1900, 199 images, browse-only. volume_search reported totalResults: 23 for Pennsylvania 1870-1900, but its summary option did not return a summary breakdown and only these 3 of 23 volumes were detailed on this page - the remainder were not examined.

### Tax records
No tax-record collection or volume was returned in this survey for Schuylkill County.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950; County Marriages 1885-1950; Probate Records 1683-1994 (0 indexed persons); Death Certificates 1906-1968; Schuylkill Church Records (test fixture, 1708-1985); Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill, 1870-1900, indexed+full text) | Marriages, probate, mine-employment, church records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Census | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ | Newspaper notices | Subscription |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | Military records | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Immigration, naturalization, military | Free/in-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes matched Pennsylvania 1870-1900; only the 3 detailed above were examined (volume_search's summary count was not returned, and a nextPageToken indicated more volumes exist beyond this page).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse (Pottsville) | Deeds, probate records, court files | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives | Probate, land, state-level records | In-person / online request |
| Local historical/genealogical societies | Local histories, church records | Contact for hours |
| Denominational archives (Catholic diocese, Lutheran/Reformed synods) | Parish registers | Contact method varies - not confirmed this survey |

## Records NOT online
Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County) and Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County) exist only as browse-only digitized images with no name index - they are online as images but not searchable by name. Land/deed books and tax records for Schuylkill County were not found in any online collection in this survey and are presumed physical-only at the courthouse pending confirmation.

## Known record losses
This survey did not retrieve a FamilySearch Wiki page confirming specific record losses for Schuylkill County; the 1890 federal census is widely known to have been destroyed, but no tool result in this run confirmed this for Pennsylvania specifically, so it is noted as general background only.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Wiki's place-specific pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the jurisdiction's Vital Records page all returned only a generic fallback article during this survey rather than Pennsylvania- or Schuylkill-specific text - re-run this survey before relying on the absence of state-specific registration dates.
- Search Schuylkill alongside the neighboring anthracite counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) - mining families moved between coal patches across county lines, and this survey found industry records (accident reports, payroll ledgers) filed under Luzerne and Lackawanna rather than Schuylkill.
- Treat the Mine Worker Employment Cards collection (imageGroupNumber 002240015) as a strong lead - it is 95% indexed and full-text searchable for Schuylkill, 1870-1900.
- catalog_search returned zero hits for Schuylkill County in this run; this is a cataloguing gap in this tool, not proof no microfilm or physical holdings exist - consult the FamilySearch Catalog directly.
- Do not assume county-level civil vital registration existed by 1870-1900 without checking a specific start date; this survey could not confirm Pennsylvania's statewide registration date because the Wiki page did not return jurisdiction-specific content.
- Use church records as the likely pre-1906 substitute for vital events, given the heavy immigrant/Catholic and Protestant population, even though this survey could not name specific parishes.

## Jurisdiction overview
- Formed 1811. County seat: Pottsville. Part of Pennsylvania's anthracite coal belt alongside Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties (Wikipedia: Coal mining in Pennsylvania).
- Economy: anthracite coal mining, dominated by companies such as the Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company and the Lehigh Valley Coal Company.
- Ethnic composition: large immigrant mining workforce - Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian.
- Key historical events: Molly Maguires activity in the 1870s; the 1869 Avondale Mine disaster (Luzerne County) prompted the state's first mine safety legislation.
- Population figures for Schuylkill County 1870-1900 could not be confirmed - place_population returned no data in this survey.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, Early 1600s Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony** was founded in 1628; **Plymouth Colony** (1620) was separate before later absorption into Massachusetts.
- Boston became the colony's principal seat after 1630. Towns and counties developed under the colony as settlement spread.
- Predominantly English Puritan settlers of the "Great Migration" (~20,000 between 1630–1640).
- Congregational (Puritan) churches were the established religion; church and civil governance were closely intertwined.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- Massachusetts **mandated towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639** — one of the earliest civil-registration requirements in America.
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (id 2061550, ~3.4M people) — searchable online.
- *Tip:* Search at the **town level**, not state-level registry, for this period.

### Church Records
- Congregational (Puritan) church records from the 1630s often predate or supplement town vital records.
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (id 1921657, ~987K people).
- A browse-only (not name-indexed) FamilySearch volume of **Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630–1700** (image group 007612045, 121 images) is digitized but must be browsed page by page.
- *Gap:* Only the Suffolk County volume was confirmed by this survey; coverage for other counties should be checked separately.

### Probate & Estate Records
- **FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (id 1678901, ~567K people) — covers the period from near the colony's founding.
- A browse-only volume of **town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698** (image group 007612044, 188 images, not name-indexed) holds land allocations, governance records, and can name residents and local officials.

### Land Records
- No name-indexed deed or grant collection for this period was confirmed by this survey. **Town proprietors' records** (above) are the identified period source for early land allocation.
- Deeds and grants may exist in repositories not surfaced here; direct inquiry with town clerks or the Massachusetts Archives is recommended.

### Census Records
- No colonial-era census exists for this period (the first U.S. federal census is 1790). Town meeting records are the nearest substitute for household/population information.

### Immigration / Passenger Lists
- The FamilySearch passenger-list collection for Massachusetts starts in **1820** — it does not cover the 1620–1700 window.
- For Great Migration immigration research, turn to **published compiled sources** (e.g., Hotten's lists or the *Great Migration* series published by NEHGS) rather than online passenger-list collections.

### Military Records
- King Philip's War (1675–1678) is the relevant conflict; no collection for it was confirmed by this survey.

### Cemetery & Newspaper Records
- Not confirmed for this period; newspapers did not yet exist in the colony in the early-to-mid 1600s.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (id 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (id 1921657); Probate Records 1635–1991 (id 1678901); Browse-only town meeting/proprietors' volume 007612044; Browse-only Suffolk church admissions volume 007612045 | Free |
| **Find A Grave** | General-purpose cemetery records | Free (not Massachusetts-curated) |

*No specific physical repository (state archives, historical society, denominational archive) was named by any tool result in this survey — confirm those directly.*

---

## Known Record Losses
No record losses for this period were confirmed by this survey. Treat collection gaps above as coverage gaps rather than confirmed losses.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search at the town level** for vital records — the 1639 mandate was town-based, not state-based.
2. **Cross-check town vital records AND church records** — church (Congregational) records from the 1630s often predate town registration and can fill gaps.
3. The **browse-only FamilySearch volumes** (town meeting/proprietors' 007612044 and Suffolk church admissions 007612045) require manual, image-by-image review — no name search is available.
4. For **Great Migration immigration** (1630s), skip online passenger-list collections (they start in 1820) and look for published compiled sources or the *Great Migration* series instead.
5. A **county- or town-specific guide** (e.g., for Suffolk, Essex, or Plymouth County) would sharpen this research further once you identify where your ancestor settled.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (early 1600s Puritan settlements, c. 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded in 1628 by the Massachusetts Bay Company; Plymouth Colony (1620) was a separate, earlier settlement later absorbed into Massachusetts (per Wikipedia's "Massachusetts Bay Colony" article).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston became the colony's principal seat after 1630.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown / Massachusetts Bay Company charter; towns and county-level divisions developed under the colony as settlement spread.
- **Population during period:** Not confirmed by this survey — `place_population` returned no data for "Massachusetts, United States" over 1620–1700; this is a tool/coverage gap, not evidence of no population data existing elsewhere.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, and early trade dominated; this shapes the prevalence of town and church records over commercial record series in this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers of the "Great Migration," per Wikipedia.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) churches were the established religion; church and civil governance were closely intertwined in these towns.
- **Key historical events:** Governor John Winthrop led the Great Migration of roughly 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (Wikipedia, "Massachusetts Bay Colony").

## Boundary changes
This survey did not confirm specific town/county boundary changes within 1620–1700; counties in Massachusetts were generally organized later in the 1600s out of the original colony territory. Treat any specific county-level boundary claim as unconfirmed until checked against a county-level locality guide.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Per Wikipedia, Massachusetts required towns to record vital events (births, marriages, deaths) starting in 1639 — one of the earliest civil-registration mandates in America. The FamilySearch Wiki's dedicated Massachusetts vital-records page could not be confirmed in this survey: the constructed URL (`Massachusetts_Vital_Records`) resolved only to a generic "Genealogy Records" template page with no Massachusetts-specific dates, so this claim rests on Wikipedia only, not the Wiki.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch's catalog shows a collection titled "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection id 2061550, ~3,456,789 people) — town-level registration, consistent with the 1639 mandate.
- **Where held:** Town clerks kept (and many still hold) the original town vital-record books; FamilySearch has digitized/indexed a large compiled collection.
- **Gaps:** No specific loss was identified by this survey; early entries can be sparse or inconsistently kept in the first years after 1639.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church (Congregational) records of baptism, admission, and burial from the 1630s predate or supplement town vital records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) churches, established from the colony's founding in 1628–1630.
- **Record types:** `volume_search` found a browse-only (not fulltext/name-indexed per its 0% searchable flag, though flagged `fulltextSearchable: true`) volume of "Congregational church admissions and baptisms," image group 007612045, 121 images, covering Suffolk County, Massachusetts, 1630–1700 — full-text searchable but not name-indexed.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has digitized this volume; original parish/church registers typically remain with the congregation or a denominational/historical archive (not named by any tool result in this survey).
- **Gaps:** This survey confirmed only the one Suffolk County volume above; coverage for other counties/towns was not returned and should be checked separately. FamilySearch's broader "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" collection (id 1921657, ~987,654 people) also covers this period.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
No federal or colonial-era census collection was returned by `collections_search` or `volume_search` for this period — unsurprising, since the first U.S. federal census is 1790, after this period. Town meeting records (below) are the nearest contemporary substitute for population/household information in the 1600s.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, and administrations.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch's "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" collection (id 1678901, ~567,890 people) covers this period from near the colony's founding.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not determinable without a specific research subject; search both wills and administration series.
- A separate browse-only volume, "Town meeting and proprietors' records" (image group 007612044, 188 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable), covering all of Massachusetts 1620–1698, holds town governance business that can name residents, landholders, and local officials outside probate and church records.

### Land records
This survey's `catalog_search` for Massachusetts returned zero hits (a cataloguing gap, not evidence land records don't exist), and no FamilySearch Wiki land-records page could be confirmed (the constructed `Massachusetts_Land_and_Property` URL was not fetched in this run). Town proprietors' records (image group 007612044, above) are the identified period source for land allocation in these early towns; deeds and grants beyond that were not confirmed by any tool in this survey.

### Military records
Not confirmed by this survey for this period; King Philip's War (1675–1678) is the relevant conflict but no record collection for it was returned by `collections_search` or `volume_search`.

### Cemetery records
No Massachusetts-specific cemetery collection was returned by the tools used. `external_links_search` surfaced a general Find A Grave link (https://www.findagrave.com/), but this is a general-purpose site, not a Massachusetts-curated resource confirmed by this survey.

### Newspaper records
No 1600s Massachusetts newspaper source was returned; newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) was returned by `external_links_search` as a general resource, not confirmed as holding period-specific content (newspapers did not yet exist in this colony in the early-to-mid 1600s).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston was the primary port for the Great Migration (1630–1640).
- **Record types:** The FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" collection (id 1784312) does **not** cover this early period — its date range starts in 1820, well after the 1620–1700 window. No passenger-list collection covering the 1620s–1690s was returned by any tool in this survey; ship-passenger documentation for the Great Migration survives mainly in published compilations (e.g., Hotten's lists), not confirmed here by any tool.

### Tax records
Not confirmed by this survey; town proprietors'/meeting records (above) are the closest substitute identified.

### Other record types
Naturalization: FamilySearch's "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" collection (id 1459213) postdates this period and is not relevant to the 1620–1700 window.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (id 2061550); "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (id 1921657); "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (id 1678901); plus browse-only volumes 007612044 (town meeting/proprietors', 1620-1698) and 007612045 (Suffolk church admissions/baptisms, 1630-1700) | Civil vital events, church events, estate records, and town governance from the colony's founding | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 total digitized volumes for Massachusetts 1620–1700 and both are detailed above — this is the complete matched set for that search, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories
No specific physical repository (state archives, historical society, denominational archive) was named by any tool result in this survey for this period; do not assume one without confirming it directly.

## Records NOT online
The browse-only town meeting/proprietors' volume (007612044) and the Suffolk church-admissions volume (007612045) are digitized by FamilySearch but are **not name-indexed** — they must be browsed image by image, with no name search. No land deed, tax, military, or pre-1820 immigration record collection for this place and period was returned by any tool, meaning any such records exist only in repositories this survey did not identify.

## Known record losses
No record loss for this place and period was stated by any tool result in this survey. Do not infer loss from the absence of a collection — treat gaps above as coverage gaps, not confirmed losses.

## Research tips
- Civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated at the **town** level starting in 1639 (Wikipedia, "Massachusetts Bay Colony") — search town-held vital records, not a state-level civil registry, for this period.
- Church (Congregational) records from the 1630s often predate or run alongside town vital records — cross-check both for the same family. The FamilySearch Wiki pages this survey attempted to fetch for Massachusetts specifically (`home`, `getting_started`, `online_records`, `research_tips`, and the constructed `Massachusetts_Vital_Records` page) all resolved only to generic template content with no Massachusetts-specific facts, so this guide could not cite Wiki-sourced specifics beyond what collections_search, volume_search, and Wikipedia provided — treat this as an open gap and re-run the Wiki lookups directly before relying on their absence.
- The browse-only volumes (007612044, 007612045) require manual, image-by-image review since they are not name-indexed.
- `catalog_search` returned zero hits for Massachusetts in this run — this is a cataloguing gap in this survey, not evidence that no catalog entries exist; retry or search the FamilySearch Catalog directly.
- Because 1630s–1690s passenger lists were not found in any collection searched, Great Migration immigration research should turn to published compiled sources rather than FamilySearch's online passenger-list collection, which only starts in 1820.

The best-documented sources are town-kept birth, marriage, and death records starting in 1639, church membership and baptism records from Congregational churches beginning in the 1630s, town meeting and land-allocation records, and probate (will and estate) records, several of which are digitized and searchable through FamilySearch, though some town and church volumes online can only be browsed page by page rather than searched by name. Several other record types people often expect for this era, like ship passenger lists, census records, cemetery indexes, and county-held land deeds, either didn't exist yet for this period or weren't confirmed to be available online in this search, so those likely require direct inquiry with town clerks, historical societies, or state archives.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma, United States (Land Run of 1889 era, c. 1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma became a state in 1907; before that it was split (1890) into the "Twin Territories" — Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory. The Unassigned Lands (opened in the April 22, 1889 Land Run) were part of Indian Territory until that run.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Prior to 1890, Indian Territory; no single civil authority governed the pre-1890 Unassigned Lands.

## Boundary Changes
- Indian Territory (to 1890) → split in 1890 into Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory ("Twin Territories") → merged into the **State of Oklahoma in 1907**. Marriages from 1890 were recorded in three newly-created Judicial Districts (Muskogee for Cherokee/Creek Nations; South McAlester for Choctaw Nation; Ardmore for Seminole/Chickasaw Nations). A family in the Unassigned Lands pre-1889 generated **no county-level civil records at all**.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Birth:** Earliest county records from 1891 (incomplete); statewide from **1908**, general compliance by 1928.
- **Marriage:** No statewide records; county-level from ~1890. Before 1890, almost no marriages were recorded — settlers often married in neighboring **Arkansas, Kansas, or Texas**.
- **Death:** Statewide from 1908, general compliance by 1928.
- **Where held:** County clerk's offices (originals); Oklahoma State Department of Health (statewide from 1908); Oklahoma State Vital Records Index at [OK2Explore](https://ok2explore.health.ok.gov/).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, cemetery records, newspaper notices/obituaries, probate records.

### Land Records ⭐ (Core Record Type for Land Run Research)
- **FamilySearch collection** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (id 1541872, ~234,567 people indexed) — directly covers the Land Run period.
- **Digitized volume:** Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907 (imageGroupNumber 005221388, 402 images, ~74% name-indexed) — this covers the actual federal homestead claims filed after the Land Run.
- **Jurisdiction note:** Land Run claims were **federal** transactions processed by the General Land Office (now Bureau of Land Management); NARA holds the original case files.

### Tribal / Indian Territory Records
- **FamilySearch collection** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (id 1987432, ~567,890 people) — relevant for any family with Indian Territory connections.
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910** (digitized volume, imageGroupNumber 005221389, 176 images, **0% indexed** — browse-only, no name search). Essential for families with tribal connections, but must be browsed image-by-image by jacket number/tribe.

### Census Records
- Standard federal decennial censuses apply: **1900 and 1910** are the key snapshots for Land Run settlers.
- No territorial/state census specific to Oklahoma was surfaced.

### Church Records
- The FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (id 1654321) covers this period.
- The FamilySearch Wiki page [Oklahoma Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Church_Records) should be consulted directly — this survey did not fetch it in detail.

### Marriage Records
- **FamilySearch collection** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (id 2134789) is indexed and covers post-Land Run marriages.
- Pre-1890: check neighboring **Arkansas, Kansas, and Texas** county courthouses, and military fort records.

### Probate and Court Records
- Held at the county/district level. The FamilySearch Wiki notes probate records "often contain the exact death date" in the 20th century — valuable when no death certificate exists.

### Cemetery Records
- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online resource, substituting for missing pre-1908 death records.
- FamilySearch Wiki: [Oklahoma Cemeteries](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Cemeteries).

### Newspaper Records
- Obituaries and marriage notices substitute for missing pre-1908 vital records.
- Resources: [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/), Chronicling America (LOC).

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early Land Records 1834–1907; Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959; County Marriages 1890–1995; Mission & Church Records 1820–1965; Homestead case files (digitized, 74% indexed); Dawes Commission jackets (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial information | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Obituaries/marriage notices | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service/pension records | Subscription |
| NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) | Federal land-entry case files, Dawes Commission records | Free |
| OK2Explore | Oklahoma State Vital Records Index (post-1908) | Free |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| County Clerk's office (per county) | Marriage bonds/licenses from ~1890; early birth/death registers from 1891 |
| Oklahoma State Dept. of Health, Vital Records (Oklahoma City) | Statewide births/deaths from 1908 |
| FamilySearch Library | Microfilmed county marriage records; published transcripts (e.g., *Oklahoma Territory Weddings*, 1983) |

---

## Records NOT Online / Known Gaps
- **Pre-1890 marriages** in the Unassigned Lands — almost none were recorded; check Arkansas, Kansas, and Texas courthouses or military fort records.
- **County-level deed books** for specific Land Run claims — digitization status not confirmed; the federal homestead case files are more accessible.
- The *1941 Guide to Public Vital Statistics Records in Oklahoma* (FamilySearch Library book 976.6 A3hr) is the authoritative inventory of what each county actually kept — consult it before assuming records survive or are lost.

---

## Key Research Tips
1. **For the actual Land Run claim**, start with the federal homestead final-proof case files (74% indexed on FamilySearch) — this is a federal, not county, transaction.
2. **Before 1890, almost no marriages were recorded** in Oklahoma — check Arkansas, Kansas, and Texas county courthouses, and fort records.
3. **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets** are browse-only with no name index — plan to search by jacket number/tribe.
4. **Use OK2Explore** (free) to check for post-1908 vital records before paying for a certified copy.
5. **Where no death record exists**, probate records often supply the exact date of death.
6. If the family may have had any **tribal connection**, the Indian Censuses & Rolls and Dawes Commission records are essential complements to the Land Run records.

---

The best starting point for a Land Run family is the **federal homestead paperwork** (the claim files processed by the federal land office, digitized and mostly name-searchable on FamilySearch), plus the **county marriage and census collections** for post-1889 family structure. For any family with Indian Territory connections, add the **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets** (browse-only). From here, the natural next step would be building a research plan targeting these specific collections.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Mississippi Territory (1798–1817, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The land that would become Alabama was organized as the **Mississippi Territory** in 1798 — the jurisdiction you must search for the year 1800. No civil jurisdiction called "Alabama" existed until the **Alabama Territory** was split off in 1817, with statehood following in 1819. Any pre-1817 record search must be conducted under "Mississippi Territory" (or simply "Mississippi") rather than "Alabama."

The territory had deep French, British, and Spanish colonial roots; early European settlement centered on Mobile Bay (1702). The Creek and Cherokee nations occupied much of the interior. Major Anglo-American in-migration surged after the Creek War of 1813–1814, right at the close of this period.

---

## Confirmed Online Record Collections (FamilySearch)

The collections search found **four** collections covering this place and period — all scoped to Mississippi broadly:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | People Indexed | Period |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 | 1919694 | 312,450 | Begins 1798 — strongest match |
| Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 | 1855293 | 245,670 | Begins 1799 |
| Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 | 1927171 | 198,340 | Covers entire period |
| Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 | 2034891 | 87,654 | Begins 1800 |

---

## Digitized, Browsable (Non-Indexed) Volumes — Direct Answer to Your Question

**None were found.** `volume_search` returned zero results for both "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi, United States" for the 1798–1819 date window. The catalog search likewise returned zero entries. This is a real coverage gap in what has been digitized and indexed for this very early territorial period — it does not mean no physical volumes survive, only that none have been catalogued in the accessible digitized-volume index.

---

## Record Type Breakdown

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
No confirmed civil registration start date for this period. No indexed vital-record collection for 1798–1817 was found. **Church records are the standard substitute** for this era.

### Census Records
Original 1800 and 1810 federal census schedules are notoriously incomplete for the Mississippi Territory. Use the **compiled census and census substitutes collection** (id 1927171) and lean on land records and tax lists as stand-ins.

### Land Records
The **Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** (id 1919694) is the most directly relevant collection found. This was a federal public-land territory, so the BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) is also worth checking for original federal patents.

### Probate / Court Records
**County Court Records, 1799–1920** (id 1855293) covers this period from 1799 and is a strong research target.

### Military Records
The Creek War (1813–1814) falls at the end of this period. No military-specific collection for this place and era was found in this survey. NARA is the standard federal repository.

### Church Records
**Church Records, 1800–1950** (id 2034891) is the best confirmed substitute for vital records. No specific denominations or congregations for the Alabama portion of the territory were confirmed by this search.

### Cemetery, Newspaper, Tax Records
No specific collections found for this exact place and period.

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search under "Mississippi" or "Mississippi Territory,"** not "Alabama," for anything before 1817–1819.
2. **Land and court records are your workhorses** here — original federal census coverage is weak for this period.
3. The four FamilySearch collections above are your confirmed online starting points.
4. FamilySearch's detailed jurisdiction-specific wiki pages for Alabama and the Mississippi Territory did not load properly during this search, so vital-records start dates and physical-archive details remain unconfirmed. Revisiting those wiki pages directly (search.familysearch.org/research-wiki) would fill those gaps.
5. No record losses were confirmed by this survey, but absence of confirmation is not the same as confirmation of survival — treat early territorial records as potentially sparse.

---

## Physical Repositories (Not Confirmed by This Survey)
No specific courthouse, state archive, or historical society holding originals for this place and period was returned by tools. The **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (archives.alabama.gov) is the standard first stop for state-held originals; for pre-1817 territorial records, the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History** may also hold relevant material.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1798, this area was claimed successively by France, Britain, and Spain (Wikipedia); it had no stable U.S. civil jurisdiction until organized as the Mississippi Territory in 1798.
- In 1817 the Mississippi Territory split, with the eastern portion becoming the Alabama Territory, which became the State of Alabama in 1819.

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

No vital, census, military, cemetery, or newspaper collection specific to the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) was found online in this survey. Only the four Mississippi-scoped FamilySearch collections above (land, county court, compiled census/substitutes, church) were confirmed to exist online and to overlap this period.

No tool result in this survey stated that any specific record series for this place and period was destroyed or lost. This absence should be read as an unconfirmed gap, not as a stated loss.

- Re-run this survey once a working connection to the jurisdiction-specific wiki pages is available, since genuine vital-records start dates, denominational detail, and record-loss history for this place remain unconfirmed here.

Looking into the Alabama area as it was around 1800, it turns out that part of the country was not yet called "Alabama" at all — it was the Mississippi Territory, organized in 1798, and Alabama itself didn't become its own place in the records until 1819. For that early period, the tools used here found four relevant historical record groups covering the wider Mississippi Territory — early land grants, county court files, census-substitute compilations, and church records — but found no digitized, browsable image volumes and no catalogued microfilm specifically for this place and period, which is a real gap in what could be confirmed today rather than proof nothing survives; also, several of FamilySearch's own detailed guide pages for this place would not load properly during this search, so some dates and local details could not be double-checked.
